clips.title: Node.js has a built-in test runner!
clips.why: Writes a first test with Node's own runner, with no Jest or Vitest installed.
look: test from node:test and assert from node:assert.
How a test passes or fails, and what the runner prints.
clips.after: Every platform package tests exactly this way, run through tsx with one root script.

clips.title: Dependency Injection Finally Explained Properly!
clips.why: The whole idea behind fakes in under two minutes: code that receives what it needs, instead of creating it.
look: The difference between code that builds its own dependencies and code that is given them.
The name for the idea, dependency injection: the code is given its dependencies from outside.
clips.after: The reporter receives the broker, so the test can hand it a fake and nothing reaches Slack.

clips.title: Dependency Injection Finally Explained Properly!
clips.why: Why that idea makes tests easy: crash-test dummies and frozen clocks, the same two fakes the lab uses.
look: A fake standing in for a real service in a test.
A frozen clock, so a test about time runs instantly.
clips.after: The lab fakes the broker with mock.fn and the clock with a now parameter, and AWS with aws-sdk-client-mock.

practice.q: Run every TypeScript test file under test/ with Node's own runner.
practice.hint: A quoted glob that reaches every folder under test/.
practice.why: --import tsx lets Node load .ts files, and the quotes let Node expand the glob the same way on every machine.

practice.q: The reporter posts to the broker. How should its test avoid touching the real Slack thread?

options.text: Pass the reporter a fake broker whose post is mock.fn
options.why: The reporter receives what it talks to, so the test hands it a recording fake and checks the calls.

options.text: Set an environment variable that makes the broker skip Slack
options.why: The test would still need a running broker and a network, and production code would grow a test switch.

options.text: Run the test only on your laptop, never in CI
options.why: A test that does not run in CI protects nothing. That is how the tag typo shipped.

practice.q: Check that the fake broker was called exactly twice.
practice.hint: mock.fn counts its calls; ask it how many.
practice.why: mock.fn records every call. callCount() gives the number, and mock.calls gives the arguments.

practice.q: In the tags test, what does ec2Mock.reset() at the start of each test prevent?

options.why: mockClient already stops every real call. reset is about the mock's own memory.

options.text: Rules and recorded calls from one test leaking into the next
options.why: Without reset, the second test could see the first test's CreateTags call or its answer, and pass or fail for the wrong reason.

options.text: TypeScript errors in the test file
options.why: reset runs while the test runs. Type errors are found by tsc before that.

practice.q: A test fails in CI. Put a good reaction in order.
items: Read + actual and - expected in the AssertionError
Open the file and line of the failing assert
Decide whether the code or the test is wrong
Fix the code, or change the test in its own explained commit
Run npm test again and see exit code 0
practice.why: The two values usually tell the whole story. A test is changed only when the test was wrong, never to make it pass.
